introduction-fighting-resume-driven-deve.core: Without guidance, engineers pick technologies by personal preference or résumé appeal, which fragments the stack and the support burden. A Tech Radar communicates which technologies are recommended, on trial, being assessed or on hold.

first_principles.problem: Every team picks a different database, queue and framework, so nobody can move between teams and the platform can't support them all.
truths: Each technology carries a support cost.
derivation: Publish a **radar** with **rings** (Adopt, Trial, Assess, Hold).

analogy.title: City building codes for roads
analogy.story: Instead of each contractor using different materials, the city recommends proven ones while still allowing pilots.
analogy.breaks: Radars that become rigid mandates stifle innovation, so keep Trial and Assess open.

example.title: Before and after a radar
flow: Radar: Postgres = Adopt, DynamoDB = Trial, MongoDB = Hold

check.a: Choosing technologies for personal career appeal rather than the organisation's needs.

the-four-rings-a-language-of-risk.core: The rings express risk. Adopt (proven, recommended default), Trial (worth using on projects that can handle some risk), Assess (worth exploring, not for production yet) and Hold (avoid for new work, being phased out).

first_principles.problem: Teams don't know whether a technology is safe for production or an experiment.
derivation: **Adopt**: use by default, with full platform support.
**Trial**: use with care in non-critical production, and learn.
**Hold**: don't start new work with it; plan migrations.

analogy.title: Traffic lights for technology
analogy.story: Green (adopt), amber (trial and assess) and red (hold) tell you how to proceed.
analogy.breaks: 'Hold' doesn't mean 'rip it out now'. Existing usage can continue during migration.

example.title: A radar excerpt
flow: Trial: Rust for data plane, Temporal

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams know where each technology stands.

example.outcome: a shared language for technology risk.

check.q: What does the 'Hold' ring mean on a tech radar?
check.a: Don't start new work with this technology; existing uses should plan to migrate away over time.

governance-moving-the-dots.core: A radar dictated by an ivory-tower architect gets ignored. Govern it collaboratively: anyone can propose a move with evidence (an RFC or PR), a cross-team group reviews it on a regular cadence, and the radar is versioned and published openly.

first_principles.problem: An architect publishes a radar nobody agrees with, so teams ignore it.
derivation: A **review group** of practitioners from several teams.

analogy.title: A community-maintained encyclopedia
analogy.story: Anyone can propose edits with sources, editors review them, and the history is public.
analogy.breaks: Too many voices can stall decisions, so set clear decision rights.

example.title: Moving a technology from Trial to Adopt
flow: Evidence: 3 production services, 9 months, low incidents
example.outcome: a radar owned by the engineering community.

check.q: Why should a tech radar be governed collaboratively?
check.a: Engineers trust and follow guidance they helped shape with evidence, rather than top-down decrees.

managing-language-proliferation.core: Adding a programming language is one of the most expensive technology decisions: build tooling, CI, libraries, security scanning, hiring, on-call expertise and long-term maintenance. Keep a small set of supported languages and a high bar for adding more.

first_principles.problem: A team writes one service in a niche language, the author leaves, and nobody can maintain it.
truths: Each language needs a full ecosystem.
Expertise concentrates in a few people.
derivation: Require an **RFC** for new languages, with a support plan.
Account for the **full cost**: tooling, CI, security, hiring.
Allow **experiments** in the Assess ring without production commitments.

analogy.title: A hospital adding a new medical specialty
analogy.story: It needs specialists, equipment, training and support staff, not just one enthusiastic doctor.
analogy.breaks: Sometimes a language truly fits better (Rust for performance), so the bar should be high but passable.

points: A high bar for new ones.

check.q: Why is adding a new programming language so costly for an organisation?
check.a: It requires tooling, CI, security scanning, libraries, hiring and long-term expertise, beyond just writing the code.
